sbh2.7:1.1: *kauśala-ālambana* and *kauśalya-ālambana* — both Sanskrit forms appear, essentially synonymous. *Kauśala* is the noun-form of *kuśala* (skillful, wholesome); *kauśalya* is the abstract noun. The doubled phrasing is unusual; one or the other could be a manuscript variant.
sbh2.7:2.4: The opening list in the source omits *saṁjñā-skandha* (perception-aggregate); supplied here by context, since the per-aggregate definitions immediately following cover all five. Editorial supplement, not whitespace rejoin — noted in the emendation audit trail.
sbh2.7:3.3: The elevenfold mode-analysis: three temporal (past/future/present), two locational (inward/outward), two qualitative (gross/subtle), two valuational (inferior/superior), two distance (far/near). Each form-instance falls under some configuration of these modes.
sbh2.7:5.2: The six perception-classes — *sa-nimitta* (with sign), *animitta* (without sign), *parītta* (limited), *mahad-gata* (expansive), *apramāṇa* (immeasurable), *ākiñcanyāyatana-saṁjñā* (perception of the base of nothingness) — map onto progressively rarefied meditation states from ordinary perception up to the third formless attainment.
sbh2.7:7.5: *sā caiṣā vedanā saṁjñā saṁskāras tac caitad-vijñānam* — 'that feeling, perception, formation — is that very consciousness.' The line points to the inseparability of consciousness from its mental content; consciousness is not a separate substrate but is constituted by what it is conscious of.
sbh2.7:8.5: The threefold definition: knowing the aggregates as distinct from one another (*nānātmakatā*), as manifold within themselves (*bahvātmakatā*), and not apprehending or conceptually constructing anything beyond them. The third condition is the soteriological hinge — skill-in-aggregates is the cognitive operation that finds *nothing beyond the aggregates*.
sbh2.7:13.6: *hetu-pratyaya-kauśalya* — 'skill-in-cause-and-condition.' Knowing that each element has its own specific causal-substrate; the eye arises from the eye-element, eye-consciousness from its own seed and lineage. The Buddha's instruction to Revata identifies this as the antidote for the cause-confused practitioner.
sbh2.7:15.9: The three conditions named here — immediate-condition (*samanantara*), object-condition (*ālambana*), and predominant-condition (*adhipati*) — are the simplified count. The fuller Yogācāra Abhidharma identifies four (adding *hetu-pratyaya*).
sbh2.7:17.2: *saṁskārā eva dharmāṇām āhārakāḥ* — 'formations alone are the carriers of dharmas.' Echoes the *idaṁ-pratyayatā* characterization (*dharmāṇām eva dharma-āhārakatvam*): same insight, slightly different formulation.
sbh2.7:18.1: *sthāna-asthāna* — literally 'place and not-place'; translates Pali *ṭhāna-aṭhāna*. The phrase from MN 115 (Bahudhātuka Sutta): 'It is a place / not a place that...' — i.e., 'it is possible / not possible that...' The skill is the cognitive ability to recognize what is causally possible and what is not.
sbh2.7:18.3: *viṣama-hetukatā* — literally 'uneven causation,' i.e., differentiated causation. Causes have specific, not arbitrary, effects: wholesome actions yield wholesome fruits, unwholesome unwished ones. This names the karmic structure of cause-and-effect.
sbh2.7:19.4: Closing synthesis: the five skills reduce to two — *svalakṣaṇa-kauśalya* (skandha-kauśalya) and *sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-kauśalya* (the remaining four). This maps onto the third and fourth investigation-subjects of the vipaśyanā method.
